en: Mayon Volcano has a perfect conical shape because its highly viscous lava cools quickly and piles up near the vent instead of flowing far.
Acidic rainwater slowly dissolves the limestone bedrock of Palawan to carve out the massive caves of the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park.
Lake Taal filled a massive crater after a gigantic prehistoric eruption emptied the underground magma chamber, causing the ground above it to collapse.
The southwest monsoon picks up moisture from the South China Sea and drops heavy rain when warm air is forced upward by the Zambales Mountains.
Magma heats underground water into high-pressure steam in Tiwi, Albay, which rises through wells to spin turbines and generate electricity.
Ancient stone walls in the Banaue Rice Terraces slow down runoff water, preventing topsoil from washing away down the steep Cordillera mountains.
Tiny coral polyps in the Sulu Sea extract calcium from seawater to build hard skeletons, gradually forming the massive Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park.
Friction at the Philippine Trench builds immense tectonic stress that eventually snaps and releases as powerful earthquakes.
The Cagayan River drops its carried sediment load upon reaching the slow-moving waters of the South China Sea, creating a wide, fertile river delta.
Dense forests on Mount Apo trap moisture from passing clouds, creating a constant mist that keeps the high-altitude ecosystems continuously hydrated.
The Earth's rotation deflects incoming winds toward a low-pressure center, causing Philippine typhoons to spin counterclockwise and draw in moist Pacific air.
Strong tidal differences between the Pacific Ocean and Samar Sea force massive volumes of water through the narrow San Bernardino Strait, creating dangerous rapids.
